entry.title: Putting Nature at the Heart of Healthcare: My Reflections from Bristol
entry.summary: By Marian Spain, CEO of Natural England In this blog, NE's Chief Executive Marian Spain reflects on her recent visit to healthcare sites in Bristol to explore how partners are incorporating nature into health and wellbeing, and discusses Natural England's …
entry.content:
By Marian Spain, CEO of Natural England

In this blog, NE's Chief Executive Marian Spain reflects on her recent visit to healthcare sites in Bristol to explore how partners are incorporating nature into health and wellbeing, and discusses Natural England's role in this.

One of the moments that stayed with me from my visit to Bristol was sitting in the greenhouse in the community allotment at Southmead Hospital and hearing how this green space on a busy hospital estate has become a place of calm, connection and recovery for patients, staff and local people. 

It was a powerful reminder that nature is not a nice-to-have in healthcare. It is part of what helps people feel well, recover well and live well. 

Across my day in Bristol, I saw how partners are bringing nature and health closer together from a specialist mental health ward, to a community-focused GP practice, to one of the country’s largest hospital estates. 

For too long, nature and health have often been treated as separate issues. But the evidence, and the lived experience of communities across England, tell us something different. Access to nature supports our physical health, our mental wellbeing and our quality of life. In fact, 90% of adults in England say green and natural spaces are good for their mental health and wellbeing. 

That is why Natural England’s new strategy, Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security, champions creating healthier places for people to live, work and spend time.   

Nature is part of our health infrastructure 

When we think about healthcare, we naturally think about hospitals, GP surgeries, medicines and treatments. All of those are vital. But we also need to recognise the role nature plays in supporting health and wellbeing long before people need clinical care. 

A walk in a local park, access to a community garden, or time spent in a wildlife-rich green space can all make a positive difference to people's lives. Yet access to nature is not experienced equally. One in five households do not have access to a green or blue space within a 15-minute walk, with the greatest inequalities often affecting more deprived communities. 

At Natural England, we want everyone to have the opportunity to access and benefit from nature, whatever their postcode. We also know that healthy natural environments can strengthen communities, support economic growth and build resilience to climate change. That is why investment in nature should be seen as investment in healthy places and people.

Seeing what's possible 

What I saw in Bristol showed how this ambition can be translated into practical action.

At Blackberry Hill Hospital, Avon and Wiltshire Mental Health Partnership NHS Trust has incorporated nature into the design and operation of the new Kingfisher Ward, recognising the role that nature-rich environments can play in supporting recovery and wellbeing. 

At Charlotte Keel Medical Centre, partners including Alive Activities and the West of England Mayoral Combined Authority have helped transform an outdoor courtyard space, demonstrating how even busy urban healthcare settings can create opportunities for connecting with nature. Over lunch they described to me what a difference it makes to the quality of breaks at work for staff, and how the courtyard garden has supported patients, some of whom now volunteer their time to look after the space.

And at Southmead Hospital, North Bristol NHS Trust is showing how a major healthcare estate can work harder for both people and Nature through community allotments, green infrastructure and biodiversity improvements that support health, wellbeing and environmental outcomes.

Each project was different, but the message was consistent: when organisations work together, nature can become part of everyday care, not an optional extra.

What impressed me most was the strength of the partnerships behind this work. Across Bristol, NHS organisations, local government, public health teams, community groups and environmental organisations are collaborating around a shared vision. Through initiatives such as green social prescribing, nature-based health projects and wider place-based partnerships, they are demonstrating how health and nature objectives can reinforce one another. 

Better outcomes for people and nature 

What gives me optimism is that this is not a choice between helping people or helping nature. The most successful examples deliver both. 

Creating greener places can improve wellbeing, support biodiversity, strengthen community resilience and help us adapt to climate change at the same time. These are not competing goals. They are mutually reinforcing.

Research suggests that regular access to greenspace could reduce GP visits by 28% and save the NHS an estimated £2.1 billion each year. At a time when health services are under increasing pressure, this is a powerful reminder that prevention matters just as much as treatment. 

To support organisations looking to take practical action, Natural England has worked with NHS England and the Centre for Sustainable Healthcare to develop the Nature for Health Resource Hub, bringing together tools, guidance and case studies that help healthcare sites improve their green spaces. 

The people I met in Bristol are showing what that looks like in practice, with commitment, imagination and care. There is much we can learn from them. 

Our commitment 

Natural England's ambition is clear: we want nature to be part of everyday life for everyone. 

That means restoring nature, improving access to green and blue spaces, and working with partners across the health, planning, environmental and local government sectors to tackle inequalities and improve wellbeing. 

The examples I saw in Bristol show what is possible. The challenge now is to build on these successes and make them the norm rather than the exception. 

Find out more

Visit the Nature for Health Resource Hub: https://nhsforest.org/resources/

Discover Green Social Prescribing tools and resources: https://socialprescribingacademy.org.uk/resources/launch-of-green-social-prescribing-innovation-community/

entry.title: Fighting Fire with Nature: How Healthy Landscapes Reduce Wildfire Risk
entry.summary: By Ruth Waters, Regional Director for the North of England, Operations Directorate, Natural England The UK is facing a growing wildfire crisis this year, with prolonged hot, dry weather fuelling blazes across our moors, farmland and urban parks. This blog …
entry.content:
By Ruth Waters, Regional Director for the North of England, Operations Directorate, Natural England

The UK is facing a growing wildfire crisis this year, with prolonged hot, dry weather fuelling blazes across our moors, farmland and urban parks. This blog explores why wildfires are becoming more frequent and severe, the role climate change plays in heightening the risk, and the wider consequences for our landscapes and water supplies. It also sets out what Natural England is doing to reduce wildfire risk on its nature reserves, and how partnerships are helping to tackle the issue on the ground.

This year we are experiencing large scale wildfires devastating the UK’s landscapes, from our moors and dales to farmland and urban parks. Prolonged hot and dry weather has provided the ideal conditions for fires to take hold, which we have also seen in mainland Europe. France has declared their ongoing wildfire situation as the worst crisis to face the country since the Second World War.

What are wildfires and why have there been so many recently?

In the UK the term “wildfire” means any uncontrolled blaze on vegetation that needs action to extinguish. Virtually all wildfires in this country are caused by human activity, from the careless (e.g. negligent use of barbecues) to the deliberate (e.g. arson), as well as the inadvertent, such as agricultural equipment faults and “managed fires” (e.g. heather/grass burning) escaping control. 

Our own records show that there have been over 240 reported wildfires this year on our most precious sites –Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) – including a 1,500 hectares fire in the Peak District (including Dove Stone RSPB reserve) which has damaged moorland valued for its blanket bog and heathland habitats, as well as breeding populations of birds such as golden plover and merlin. This fire was started by people setting off fireworks – so far one person from Greater Manchester has been charged with multiple criminal offences relating to the incident. 

Most recently a fire at Dunwich Heath in Suffolk engulfed some 150 hectares, with the National Trust estimating it could take 25 years for the site to recover. At the height of the fire over 100 firefighters were needed to bring it under control, with hundreds of homes and caravans evacuated.

The consequences of climate change

Climate change is heightening the risk of wildfires. Extreme weather events are increasing, and like 2025, this summer has seen prolonged periods of dry weather alongside a series of record-breaking heatwaves across the world.

On 29th July, the Environment Agency announced that more than half of England was in drought. Looking more widely, Europe has warmed almost twice as fast as the global average. A warming atmosphere combined with prolonged dry conditions accelerates moisture removal from vegetation and soils. This creates an abundance of dry fuel for blazes to take hold and spread.

It’s not just the direct destruction from the fires themselves that we need to deal with. The bare, dry soil they leave behind repels water from the next rainfall event, causing run-off that can lead to soil erosion and flooding. In addition, sediment flowing into watercourses adds to the treatment costs for drinking water (over 70% of our drinking water comes from our uplands), which is then passed onto customers through higher water bills.

What is Natural England doing right now?

Reducing wildfire risks and impacts on our National Nature Reserves

As a landowner ourselves, we continue to put measures in place on our National Nature Reserves (NNRs) to adapt and respond to increasing wildfire risk.  We are responsible for the management of over 130 NNRs – not all are at high risk from wildfire, but many are and climate change will see more of our NNRs at risk of either accidental or deliberate fires. We have developed wildfire emergency plans for our high-risk reserves that have information that will help our staff and the fire service in the event of fire such as access points, key-holders and muster points.

We ensure staff on high-risk sites have received specialist vegetation fire training provided through LANTRA and the Forestry Commission, and that we have the specialist equipment available to support fire and rescue services and to fight minor fires ourselves.

We incorporate fire reduction measures into our core site management. This reduces the ‘fuel’ available to a fire. For example, using firebreaks of broadleaved woodland and vegetation management such as grazing and cutting to stop a fire from spreading.

We use more active restoration measures to give nature a helping hand, like stone dams or bunds to hold back water in our peatlands, keeping water in the landscape for longer. Maintaining fire breaks and access routes also helps move firefighting equipment to isolated parts of our estate.

Prevention is better than cure

On our most vulnerable sites during periods of high fire risk, we present a more active, visible warden presence, supported by signage and publicity. This isn’t just aimed at deterring those who start fires deliberately, but at reducing the risk from accidental fires caused by discarded cigarettes or glass bottles or people using disposable barbeques.

Experience has demonstrated that where we are able to provide a high-profile warden presence that engages with the public constructively, fire incidents are reduced. In extreme cases we can temporally reduce access to an area to protect the public.

Working in partnership

We work with partners across England on a number of wildfire issues.

Nationally Natural England administers the Nature for Climate Peatland Grant Scheme, working with landowners and over 100 partners to rewet and restore peatlands, which hold more water in the landscape making it more difficult for fire to spread. Natural England are also part of the England and Wales Wildfire Forum which works to expand understanding of wildfires to reduce the impact they have.

At a local level, Natural England is a member of the Dorset Heaths Partnership which has been exploring ways to tackle wildfire issues since 2007. The Partnership includes site managers, the Fire and Rescue Service and the police. 

The partners operate a WhatsApp group to both rapidly notify managers of a wildfire incident but also to coordinate water bowsers, equipment to cut and extend firebreaks and to advise the emergency services of site hazards and sensitive areas.

A dedicated partnership warden team works with local people, especially dog walkers, to rapidly report incidents and help engage with those that are unaware of the dangers of wildfire. Fire access points are all mapped and coded for ease of incident reporting and, more recently, QR codes have been added so the emergency services can get to the right locations quickly.

What Next?

A key finding of the latest adaptation report from the Climate Change Committee (CCC) - A Well-Adapted UK, is that coordination is lacking in a range of areas to manage the increasing risks to society from climate change. The report recommends the UK Government facilitates coordinated assessment and management of cascading climate risks between sectors and joint planning of the responses to extreme events (including wildfires).

At Natural England we have established a new Wildfire Project Group to co-ordinate the organisation’s work on wildfires, which is multi-faceted given our statutory duties as well as our landowner role. This group will review our procedures and ensure we continue to use the best available evidence to inform our decision-making and advice to Government. It will also consider our current approaches to more short-term wildfire mitigation measures, against the backdrop of our overall aim of recovering our ecosystems to bring long-term resilience to the growing challenges of climate change.  

Natural England is also working closely with Defra, the Forestry Commission and Environment Agency on a co-ordinated approach to wildfire planning and response, feeding up to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) as overall department lead for wildfire.

entry.title: Explore More for Less: Affordable East Midlands Nature Days Out
entry.summary: This summer, if you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days …
entry.content:
This summer, if you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days out in the East Midlands! 

 The school holidays are here, and the East Midlands has some special places to explore - many of them free or very nearly so. Whether you're after a coastal walk, ancient woodland, or a magical trail through the forest, there's something for every family this summer. Here are five of our favourite affordable days out in nature across the East Midlands.

Lincolnshire Coronation Coast National Nature Reserve 

Stretching for almost 30 kilometres along the Greater Lincolnshire coast, the Lincolnshire Coronation Coast National Nature Reserve (NNR), the first in the King’s Series of NNRs, is free to visit. The reserve brings together sand dunes, saltmarsh, mudflats and freshwater marshes of international importance, and is home to natterjack toads, grey seals, and a spectacular array of birds.

The reserve also forms part of the King Charles III England Coast Path (KCIIIECP), so you can combine a walk along one of England's great national trails with a chance to experience some truly special wildlife habitat. Cleethorpes and Mablethorpe neighbour the reserve, making it easily accessible and with plenty of options to grab some fish and chips before you head home!

Getting there: The reserve is accessible from several points along the Lincolnshire coast. Cleethorpes has a train station with regular services from Lincoln and Doncaster. Mablethorpe is accessible by bus from Lincoln.

Clumber Park, Nottinghamshire (National Trust) 

Nestled in the ancient forest of Sherwood, Clumber Park is a picturesque 3,800-acre expanse of parkland, heath, woodland and lake that was once the country estate of the Dukes of Newcastle. This summer, it's easier than ever to get there without a car, and cheaper too.

A new daily bus service links Worksop Train Station, Worksop Bus Station and Clumber Park, running every day from 25 July to 6 September 2026. Return tickets cost just £3 per person and include free admission to the park.

National Trust members, under-fives, and visitors arriving at Worksop by train with a valid rail ticket all travel free and enter the park at no charge. Under 16s are free from 1 to 31 August.

Once you're there, the National Trust’s Summer of Play programme offers six interactive play zones, free ukulele workshops, storytelling sessions and much more, all included with entry. This year also sees Clumber take part in a nationwide National Trust partnership with Pokémon, meaning there’s enough entertainment for children of all ages.

Getting there: Bus service operates from Worksop Train Station (served by trains from Nottingham and Sheffield). Return bus ticket (£3) includes park entry. Service runs daily 25 July – 6 September 2026.

Bradgate Park and Swithland Wood National Nature Reserve, Leicestershire 

Just a short journey from Leicester city centre, Bradgate Park is one of the region's most loved wild spaces. Spanning 438 hectares of rugged, ancient landscape, the park features ancient oak trees, roaming deer and some of the very oldest and rarest rocks on earth. The lower part of the park is accessible via a tarmac carriageway suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs, and the visitor centre tells the story of the estate's fascinating natural and human history. Both the park and the visitor centre are free to enter.

This summer, families can also take part in the Moths and Butterflies Trail, running until 23 August 2026. Follow the path from Newtown Linford to the visitor centre, spot painted examples of the moths and butterflies found at Bradgate and Swithland Wood, collect hidden letters and solve the mystery moth, then claim your sticker prize at the visitor centre. It's a lovely free activity for children of all ages.

Getting there: Newtown Linford is served by bus from Leicester city centre (Arriva service 120 from St Margaret's Bus Station). The park entrance at Newtown Linford is a short walk from the bus stop. Bradgate Park also has three car parks, charges apply.

Forestry England Sherwood Pines, Nottinghamshire  

Take a stroll into the deep dark wood for a day of adventure at Sherwood Pines. The forest is free to enter, with something for everyone: three waymarked walking trails, cycling trails for all abilities, and play areas throughout the woodland. 

Families with young children will love the Gruffalo sculptures dotted through the trees and the Room on the Broom interactive trail, where children can help Witch find her lost hat, bow and wand while exploring the forest. Room on the Broom trail packs are available from the visitor centre for £4.

Getting there: Sherwood Pines is near Edwinstowe, Nottinghamshire. The nearest train station is Mansfield (Robin Hood Line from Nottingham), with onward bus connections via the number 14 or 15 bus from Mansfield bus station (next to the train station). If driving, car park charges apply to non-members.

The Pennine Bridleway, Derbyshire 

For an accessible taste of Peak District scenery, head to Middleton Top, the southernmost start point of the Pennine Bridleway. This family-friendly, mostly flat trail follows the route of the old Cromford and High Peak Railway, and is suitable for walking, cycling or wheeling, making it a great option for families with pushchairs or wheelchair users. There's a visitor centre, café and toilets on site, plus a picnic area at the adjacent Redhill Quarry Nature Reserve. The historic Engine House is open some weekends (fees apply). 

Alternatively, further along the route, the picturesque village of Hayfield offers access to a short, one-mile stretch of the Sett Valley Trail, also following a former railway line through wildlife-rich woodland. The trail runs alongside the village bus station, with a handful of cafes, pubs and shops, plus a picnic area and toilets nearby.

If you'd rather see more of the Peak District without the walk, the Stagecoach Peak Sightseer open-top bus is worth considering. Running daily until 19 September, it offers hop-on, hop-off travel between destinations including Chatsworth, Bakewell, Castleton and Hathersage, so you can enjoy the views and dip into a village or two without lacing up your walking boots. It isn't a free option (a family day ticket costs £38), but it's a flexible way to see a lot of the National Park in a single day.

Getting there: Middleton Top is on local bus routes, with connections from Cromford, Matlock and Matlock Bath train stations. Hayfield's Sett Valley Trail runs alongside Hayfield bus station. The Peak Sightseer can be joined at various stops including Chatsworth and Bakewell. There are also morning journeys from Chesterfield train station and South Sheffield to Chatsworth with return journeys late afternoon. 

A few more favourites 

Of course, this is not an exhaustive list and there are so many more great places to get out in nature on our doorstep that we couldn’t possibly name them all. Here are a few more though which are family friendly and free to enter:

  • Whisby Nature Park near Lincoln (Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust) 
  • Attenborough Nature Reserve near Nottingham (Nottinghamshire Wildlife Trust) 
  • Frampton Marsh near the Wash (RSPB) 
  • Sherwood Forest National Nature Reserve in Nottinghamshire (RSPB) 
  • Sandilands Nature Reserve near Sutton on Sea (National Trust) 
  • Watermead Country Park near Leicester 
  • Allestree Park in Derby 

Or for some options even closer to home Local Nature Reserves are places valued for their wildlife or geology, designated by local councils for people to enjoy and learn from. Find your nearest one: Local Nature Reserves (England) | Natural England Open Data Geoportal

With the recent dry, hot weather, wildfire risk is high across the countryside. Please pack a picnic instead of a barbecue, take your rubbish home with you, and if you spot an unattended fire, get to a safe place and call 999. 

Remember to always follow the Countryside Code when you’re out and about in nature! 

The Countryside Code is a simple guide to helping everyone enjoy the outdoors responsibly while protecting the natural environment. It encourages visitors to respect other people, protect plants, animals and habitats, and leave gates, paths and property as they find them. By following the Countryside Code, we can all play our part in keeping nature accessible, safe and enjoyable for everyone, while helping to conserve the landscapes and wildlife that make our countryside so special.

entry.title: Water and Wellbeing: The People And Nature Blue Spaces Report
entry.summary: By Fränze Kibowski, Senior Specialist - Social Sciences This blog explains the results of the recent People and Nature Blue Spaces Report, discussing how we interact with places like beaches, rivers and lakes, while looking at how the findings will …
entry.content:
By Fränze Kibowski, Senior Specialist - Social Sciences

This blog explains the results of the recent People and Nature Blue Spaces Report, discussing how we interact with places like beaches, rivers and lakes, while looking at how the findings will influence Natural England's work.

When was the last time you spent time outside near the sea, or a river? 

Spending time in ‘blue spaces’ - places where water is a key part of the environment, such as rivers, lakes, canals, beaches and the coast – can have positive effects on our mental and physical wellbeing.

A new report from Natural England and NatCen explores how people use these spaces, what they value about them and what can make it easier for more people to visit.  

Blue spaces are important to many people 

The research found that almost half of adults in England (47%) visited a blue space in the previous month, highlighting the important role these places play in people’s lives and their connection with nature. 

Participants consistently described blue spaces as calming and restorative. Many described visiting rivers, lakes and the coast when they wanted time to relax, reflect or cope with stress.  

Blue spaces support a wide range of activities and experiences, from everyday walks and  exercise to socialising with family and friends, sightseeing, wildlife watching and connecting to nature. 

Making blue spaces accessible for everyone 

While many people enjoy blue spaces, the research found that opportunities to visit are not experienced equally across the population. 

At Natural England, our ambition is for access to nature to be a normal part of everyday life for everyone. This research helps us better understand the barriers some people face in visiting blue spaces and identifies opportunities to make these valuable natural environments more accessible, welcoming and inclusive.

A range of factors can influence how often people visit, including access to transport (in particular a car), proximity to blue spaces, health considerations and wider socio-economic circumstances. Because many blue spaces are destinations people travel to rather than places encountered during everyday routines, transport and accessibility can play an even more important role than with green spaces.

Quality matters

The condition of blue spaces was another important theme throughout the research. 

Litter, pollution, poor maintenance and concerns about water quality can discourage people from spending time there. Safety was also important, particularly in winter when reduced daylight can make some places feel less accessible.

People said they would be more likely to use blue spaces if they were clean, well maintained, easy to access and felt safe throughout the year.

Supporting greater engagement 

The findings from the country-wide  Adults’ People and Nature Survey and more in-depth focus groups both show that blue spaces have an important role to play alongside green spaces. By improving access and quality, more people can experience the health, wellbeing and nature benefits that these environments provide. 

This report highlights several ways to help more people benefit from blue spaces. These include improving accessibility and transport links, investing in maintenance and environmental quality, and addressing barriers faced by groups who currently visit less often.  

This summer, Natural England will be sharing affordable ideas and inspiration to help people access and enjoy local green and blue spaces. Whether it’s exploring a stretch of the King Charles III England Coast Path, taking a walk along a local river, so spending time beside a canal or lake, there are plenty of opportunities to enjoy the benefits of blue spaces.

Wherever you choose to visit, please help protect these special places by following the Countryside Code and, if you're heading out on the water or to the coast, the Paddlers' Code and Marine and Coastal Wildlife Code, helping us all to Respect, Protect and Enjoy our blue spaces.

The full report and a summary report can be found here.

entry.title: Explore More for Less: Affordable West Midlands Nature Days Out
entry.summary: This summer, if you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days …
entry.content:
This summer, if you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days out in the West Midlands! 

Summer is here, and the West Midlands is home to some of England's best-kept secrets when it comes to affordable, accessible nature. Whether you're after dramatic upland views, ancient woodland, or a wetland reserve buzzing with wildlife, there's something here for every family, every budget, and every level of mobility.

We've picked out five brilliant places to explore this summer, all either free to enter or costing very little, and all reachable without a car if you plan ahead.

Cheltenham Escarpment National Nature Reserve (NNR), Gloucestershire

Better known locally as Leckhampton Hill and Charlton Kings Common, this is one of England's newest NNRs, designated in June 2026, and home to the legendary 'Devil's Chimney'. This striking limestone pillar is thought to have been left standing by quarry workers. Although local folklore insists it was built by the Devil himself, so he'd have somewhere to sit and throw stones at churchgoers below. Who are we to say? But we do know the site contains the thickest inland sequences of Jurassic limestone and supports nationally important limestone grassland, home to wildflowers and 33 recorded butterfly species including the rare Duke of Burgundy.

The hill has panoramic views over Cheltenham, the Severn Vale and the Welsh hills and is part of the King's Series of National Nature Reserves, created to mark the Coronation of His Majesty King Charles III. Entry is free, and there are paths and tracks that the whole family can explore, including a 3km walk suitable for pushchairs and wheelchair users.

Getting there: There are four car parks on site, at Daisy Bank Road and Hartley Lane. The hill is a short distance from Cheltenham town centre and well served by local buses.

Sutton Park National Nature Reserve (NNR), Birmingham 

One of the largest urban parks in Europe, Sutton Park is a 2,100-acre National Nature Reserve just six miles from Birmingham city centre, and it's completely free to visit. Inside you'll find heathland, woodland, seven lakes, and even grazing cattle and wild ponies. There's a 5-kilometre walking route and two playgrounds, making it ideal for younger children. The visitor centre has toilets, baby changing facilities and maps to help you find your way.

The park forms part of Purple Horizons, a Natural England-led nature recovery project working to connect Sutton Park with Cannock Chase, creating a wildlife corridor across the West Midlands urban fringe.

Getting there: The Town Gate entrance is a seven-minute walk from Sutton Coldfield train station, which is accessible via a twenty-minute train from Birmingham New Street. Buses 6, 935, 937, X3 and X5 also stop nearby.

Hall Green Naturehood Trail, Birmingham (National Trust and Go Jauntly)

For an option even closer to Birmingham city centre, try the Hall Green Naturehood Trail, a free 4.7km circular walk created by the National Trust in partnership with the Go Jauntly app. The route links green and blue spaces across Hall Green, starting at the historic Sarehole Mill, one of Birmingham's last two working watermills.

Along the way you'll pass the River Cole, wildflower meadows, and Trittiford Mill Pool, home to swans, ducks and dragonflies. The trail includes fun prompts for families, from birdwatching tips to "cloud-spotting." Download the free app for step-by-step directions or print the PDF guide in advance.

Getting there: The walk starts at Sarehole Mill, with a bus stop directly outside served by routes 5 and 11C Outer Circle.

Brandon Marsh Nature Reserve, Coventry (Warwickshire Wildlife Trust) 

Brandon Marsh is a Warwickshire Wildlife Trust reserve known for its pools, reedbeds and woodland, and home to kingfishers, otters and muntjac deer.  

Two surfaced trails, the Kingfisher Trail and the Woodpecker Trail, make this a great choice for buggies, wheelchairs and mobility scooters, and the reserve even offers free mobility scooter loans if you call ahead. Nine bird hides give you the chance to get up close to the wildlife, and the visitor centre has a café, shop and picnic area to round off your visit. 

Entry costs £4.75 for adults, with concessions and family tickets available, and it's free for Wildlife Trust members. 

Getting there: Brandon Marsh is on Brandon Lane, Coventry, with an on-site car park. Bike parking is also available.

Stiperstones Landscape National Nature Reserve (NNR), Shropshire

Stiperstones covers 1,562 hectares of dramatic upland heath, ancient woodland and rare geology along the Shropshire Hills. It's part of the King's Series and is managed by a partnership including Natural England, Forestry England, Shropshire Wildlife Trust and local community groups.

Entry is free. Start at the NNR car park, where you'll find a 650-metre all-ability trail alongside longer walking routes if you fancy tackling the full ridge. Keep an eye out for the legendary Devil's Chair, a rock formation shattered by ice-age freezing that has inspired ghost stories for centuries, and look out for red grouse, emperor moths and the increasingly rare bilberry bumblebee along the way.

If you'd rather leave the car at home, the Shropshire Hills Shuttle Bus runs every weekend from May to September, taking in the Long Mynd, Carding Mill Valley and Stiperstones itself, with adult tickets from £2 and free travel for under-16s. It's a brilliant, low-cost way to see some of Shropshire's best scenery without worrying about parking.

Getting there: The reserve is 3km east of the A488, with car parking available at the main NNR car park, the Bog, and Snailbeach. Alternatively, catch the Shropshire Hills Shuttle Bus from Church Stretton. 

A couple more favourites 

Chapter Meadows Nature Reserve in Worcester sits alongside the River Severn, just a mile from Worcester Foregate Street train station. Painswick Beacon in Gloucestershire is the site of an Iron Age hillfort, standing 283 metres high with some of the best 360-degree views in the Cotswolds. Painswick Beacon is on a bus route, and you can download the Gloucestershire Walks app for a map to guide you.

Or for some options even closer to home Local Nature Reserves are places valued for their wildlife or geology, designated by local councils for people to enjoy and learn from. Find your nearest one: Local Nature Reserves (England) | Natural England Open Data Geoportal 

With the recent dry, hot weather, wildfire risk is high across the countryside. Please pack a picnic instead of a barbecue, take your rubbish home with you, and if you spot an unattended fire, get to a safe place and call 999. 

Remember to always follow the Countryside Code when you’re out and about in nature! 

The Countryside Code is a simple guide to helping everyone enjoy the outdoors responsibly while protecting the natural environment. It encourages visitors to respect other people, protect plants, animals and habitats, and leave gates, paths and property as they find them. By following the Countryside Code, we can all play our part in keeping nature accessible, safe and enjoyable for everyone, while helping to conserve the landscapes and wildlife that make our countryside so special.

entry.title: Finding the unfindable: BBC films Natural England's dive team on Cornwall's ancient seabed after the discovery of a new seaweed species
entry.summary: By Angela Gall - Marine Senior Officer, Devon, Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Area Team Off the south coast of Cornwall, in the cold, clear water, lie some of England's least-known natural treasures: the maerl beds. Earlier this summer, our …
entry.content:
By Angela Gall - Marine Senior Officer, Devon, Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Area Team

Off the south coast of Cornwall, in the cold, clear water, lie some of England's least-known natural treasures: the maerl beds. Earlier this summer, our dive team's work there caught the attention of the BBC, who came to film one of the most significant discoveries our surveys have produced, a species of seaweed new to science, alongside several other rare and long-absent finds. This blog looks at what was found, why these ancient, fragile beds matter, and what the work to understand and protect them means for the future.

In the cold, clear water off the south coast of Cornwall lies one of England's most extraordinary and least-known natural treasures: Maerl beds. The pink, branching rhodoliths - free-living, calcified red seaweed - lie loose across the sediment in interlocking drifts, building up over centuries into structures that support an astonishing wealth of marine life.

Earlier this summer, the BBC came to film our dive team at work on these remarkable habitats to break the news about one of the most exciting scientific discoveries our surveys have ever produced.

A species new to science, found right on our doorstep

Our underwater surveys here have uncovered something very special: a tiny red seaweed, a species of Ceramium (pincer weed), that is completely new to science. Just a few millimetres across, its tiny size means it has never been formally identified until now. It took our divers bringing up living fragments to the surface, careful cultivation in the lab, and DNA sequencing to finally confirm what it was.

It's a finding that has delighted world-leading seaweed taxonomy authority Professor Christine Maggs, who told us: "I first encountered this tiny Ceramium in the early 1980s, and I have been wondering about it ever since. Natural England's surveys finally provided the missing piece of a scientific puzzle I've been trying to solve for most of my career."

The Ceramium wasn't the only significant find. The surveys also recorded Ulva rigida, a green sea lettuce never previously confirmed in the UK; Neofolia rosea (little rosy tongue weed), only found once before in the UK, also on in the Fal Estuary; and Bonnemaisonia clavata, a delicate red seaweed not seen in British waters since the 18th century. Far from being fringe curiosities, their presence reveals the richness of life these maerl beds support, why they matter and what condition they are in.

Our Senior Marine Officer Angie Gall explains: "We've already recorded more than 380 species living on the surface of the maerl beds, and that's only the beginning. Many more species live within the maerl itself or appear at different times of year."

The BBC joins the dive team

On an overcast morning in early June, BBC News journalist Harriet Bradshaw and camera operator Tony Jolliffe joined us aboard our survey vessel off the Cornish coast to film our dive team in action, surveying the maerl beds. Our team of scientific divers were also joined by seaweed expert Francis Bunker, who first identified the new Ceramium species during the original surveys.

The BBC had already visited the Natural History Museum, where they filmed Professor Maggs and Professor Juliet Brodie, exploring the archival and scientific process behind formally describing a new species. Old pressed specimens and historical records are all part of the long paper trail that connects a new find to everything that came before it. Our filming on and under the water completed the picture, showing the fieldwork, the marine habitats and the people behind the discovery.

What happened back in the field lab that evening underlines how much these beds still have to reveal. Examining samples brought up from the seabed, Francis found another specimen of the same Ceramium, and this time it carried tetrasporangia: specialised reproductive structures (sporangia) found in certain seaweeds (particularly red algae), which had not been found before.

Why maerl matters

Maerl beds are among the most biodiverse shallow-water habitats in the entire north-east Atlantic. The pink, twiggy rhodoliths that form these beds grow about half a millimetre a year and some beds in the Fal Estuary are estimated to be up to 4,000 years old, pre-dating much of recorded British history. They act as nurseries for young fish and shellfish, provide shelter for a vast range of marine life, and lock away carbon in their sediments.

The vast majority of England's maerl is concentrated along Cornwall's south coast, and Natural England's work since 2023 has already led to the discovery of extensive areas of previously unknown maerl beds within and around the Falmouth Bay to St Austell Bay Special Protection Area - a reminder that even in well-studied waters, significant ecosystems can remain hidden. These are, as Angie describes them, "living archives of our natural history."

Yet they are also fragile. Physical disturbance, pollution, and climate change all pose ongoing threats. As Francis Bunker, who discovered the new Ceramium, reflected: "Finding species new to science in our waters is thrilling. But it also shows how much biodiversity is still hidden in these beds and what we stand to lose if these habitats are damaged before we've fully understood them."

Where the work goes next

The BBC story is part of a much bigger picture. Over the past two years, Natural England has been working intensively with partners to understand, map, and protect Cornwall's maerl beds. This has included detailed dive surveys and seabed mapping across the Falmouth Bay to St Austell Bay Special Protection Area and Fal and Helford Special Area of Conservation and the publication of the Cornwall Maerl Conservation Action Plan 2025–2030.

The Action Plan was developed through the UK's first dedicated Maerl Forum, led by Natural England, bringing together scientists, marine managers, conservationists, and policymakers. It sets out a shared framework for protecting Cornwall's maerl over the next five years, covering everything from monitoring and water quality to improving sustainability of fishing in the area, research into habitat restoration and public engagement.

Whole genome sequencing at the University of Exeter has mapped distinct maerl populations across south-west Britain, discovering a genetically unique population found only in St Mawes. This research, to be published soon, is directly informing advice to marine managers and contributing to national programmes including the ‘30by30’ global commitment to protect and properly care for 30% of land and sea by 2030, and the UK government’s Marine Protected Area Network Review.

There is still much more to discover and much more to do. But what we do know is that maerl is a precious, important and irreplaceable habitat that is slowly giving up its secrets, with further exciting discoveries likely. As these latest findings show, the rewards for this careful, patient scientific work can be extraordinary: species hidden for centuries, or unknown to science entirely, waiting to be found in the waters just off our coast.

Look out for the BBC News story on YouTube. To find out more about our maerl work, see the Cornwall Maerl Conservation Action Plan and visit the Cornwall Maerl website.

entry.title: Otterly Brilliant: Occupational Therapy Supporting Nature-Based Health Delivery and Site Improvements
entry.summary: By Esther Smith, Senior Officer, Health and Environment (North East and Yorkshire) This blog outlines the importance of green spaces in improving health and wellbeing, with a focus on occupational therapy, while showcasing some of the amazing projects in this …
entry.content:
By Esther Smith, Senior Officer, Health and Environment (North East and Yorkshire)

This blog outlines the importance of green spaces in improving health and wellbeing, with a focus on occupational therapy, while showcasing some of the amazing projects in this field.

Natural England's Strategy aims to improve health and wellbeing by enabling more people to connect with, access and benefit from nature. As part of this, we are working with NHS organisations providing expert advice and early-stage funding to help develop nature-based health initiatives.

Across the NHS, there is growing interest in nature-based approaches and therapies that support physical and mental health. High-quality green spaces can play an important role in promoting wellbeing, aiding recovery, and helping to reduce health inequalities.

Oliver Harmar, Chief Strategy Officer at Natural England, said:

"Nature really is our Natural Health Service, and its economic and social value in delivering health benefits is huge.  Being in and around green spaces is genuinely transformative for both our mental and physical wellbeing, easing anxiety, lifting our mood, and supporting recovery after illness. The programmes we're seeing in Bradford and beyond show exactly why nature-based approaches deserve a central place in how we think about health. With a 10-year gap in life expectancy across the Bradford district alone, and the NHS's 10-year plan rightly prioritising prevention, partnerships connecting people with nature offer a real opportunity to close that gap, delivering one of the most powerful, cost-effective ways to support people's health and wellbeing."

Green spaces offer powerful settings for occupational therapy, supporting people to manage everyday activities whether they are recovering from illness, living with a disability, facing mental health challenges or adapting to later life. Operational colleagues across our area teams are increasingly working alongside occupational therapists as part of our health and environment programme. The examples below show how these partnerships are opening up nature to more people through their occupational therapy treatment.

Bradford Green Therapy Programme

The Green Therapy initiative is woven into the occupational therapy curriculum and embedded across Bradford District Care Trust more widely. It brings together health, environmental and community organisations including Aire Rivers Trust, Forestry England, Canal & River Trust, Yorkshire Dales National Park Authority, YorGreen CIC, Word Up North and Pieces Project. With initial funding from Natural England for a student placement, the initiative has since expanded to include:

  • The Nature in Mind programme with Bradford and Craven Mind, creating two nature support worker posts and four nature-based groups supporting participants weekly. 
  • A partnership with the specialist Mother and Babies Team to develop a new nature-based intervention.
  • Funding from the Centre for Sustainable Healthcare for a Nature Ranger role, supporting activities across inpatient mental health sites while strengthening links with local nature recovery initiatives.
  • Weekly allotment groups, with plans underway to develop two more sites.
  • Workforce development, through a nature therapy training programme developed with Mind, alongside Horticultural training delivered by Thrive.

Kelly Barker, Chief Operating Officer at Bradford District Care NHS Foundation Trust, said:

“I have seen first-hand the positive impact that nature-based therapies can have on both the people who use our services and the staff who support them. These approaches help people build confidence, improve wellbeing, and reconnect with their communities. By bringing people together in nature, we are supporting healthier lives and stronger communities. I am incredibly proud of the colleagues, volunteers and partners making this work possible.”

Watch this video to find out more.

A participant in the allotment group said:

“A positive response for my mental health... I look forward to the allotment each week giving me a purpose to get up in a morning...! I love being at one with nature, bird watching, music, collecting insects, photography, crafts, art, walking, planting, and canoeing!”

Building the case for green therapy

Natural England is partnering with a range of organisations to develop and expand green therapy approaches:

  • A Northumbria University student placement is uncovering new nature-based opportunities within National Nature Reserves.
  • South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust is exploring occupational therapy placements to strengthen its Active Hospitals programme and deliver on its Green Plan.
  • A partnership with the University of Worcester is bringing outdoor classrooms, a community orchard and future nature prescription initiatives with the RSPB to life.
  • At Newcastle's NHS Freeman Hospital, the Centre for Sustainable Health is working alongside Occupational Therapists to help patients reconnect with the natural world through the power of scent.
  • Occupational Therapy students from the University of Huddersfield are testing new approaches to connecting children with nature, producing recommendations, training resources and transition materials to shape community engagement through the National Health Innovation Campus and developing a nature connection pack with the Canal & River Trust.

Looking ahead: driving innovation

Two events planned for autumn 2026 will help shape the future of green therapy. A roundtable will bring together NHS organisations, universities and placement hosts to explore new opportunities, while a wider stakeholder webinar will showcase green occupational therapy projects, research and partnerships from across the country.

Together, these reflect growing momentum behind nature-based approaches in occupational therapy and the power of partnership to improve health outcomes and deepen connections between people, places and communities.

entry.title: Where nature strengthens community: celebrating England's first accredited Nature Towns
entry.summary: By Marian Spain, Chief Executive, Natural England In this blog, NE Chief Executive Marian Spain reflects on her visit to Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole (BCP), alongside senior leaders from The National Lottery Heritage Fund and the National Trust, to see …
entry.content:
By Marian Spain, Chief Executive, Natural England

In this blog, NE Chief Executive Marian Spain reflects on her visit to Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole (BCP), alongside senior leaders from The National Lottery Heritage Fund and the National Trust, to see firsthand the amazing benefits of the Nature Towns and Cities programme.

What makes a great place to live? Increasingly, the answer includes easy access to nature. In Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole (BCP), residents benefit from an extensive network of parks, green spaces and coastal habitats; spaces that support health, wellbeing and community life, and help people connect with nature close to home.

But what does it really take to make that happen at scale, and to sustain it? That was the question in my mind this week when I joined Eilish McGuinness, Chief Executive of the National Lottery Heritage Fund, and Hilary McGrady, Director General of the National Trust, the founding partners of Nature Towns and Cities to visit BCP Council and see firsthand what becomes possible when local ambition meets national partnership.

A national leader for urban nature

In 2025, BCP became the first place to receive official Nature Towns accreditation. This recognition reflects more than a decade of work embedding nature into planning, public health, climate resilience, and community life, with results to show for it. It goes far beyond planting trees or maintaining parks.

Since 2023, BCP Council and its local partners have gone further still, helping to shape the Nature Towns and Cities programme at a national level, acting as pioneer and mentor to urban areas across the country.

Transforming parks and communities

Across a population of 409,000, BCP and its partners are delivering an ambitious green transformation. The council is upgrading fourteen urban parks into multi-functional community hubs, blending nature-friendly planting with community cafes and volunteering opportunities. The BCP Nature Pledge empowers residents, businesses, and schools to turn their own outdoor spaces into wildlife havens. And major landscape-scale projects including the Stour Valley Park and Littletown Greenway now connect fragmented green corridors across the area.

Each of BCP's parks and green spaces generates around £20 of health and wellbeing value per visit, underlining the economic as well as social case for this investment.

Nature as preventative infrastructure

BCP faces real challenges. The area has significant health and social inequalities, including a nine-year gap in male life expectancy between its most and least deprived communities. Access to green space is uneven, with canopy cover lowest in some of the borough's most disadvantaged neighbourhoods.

The council increasingly views nature not as an amenity but as preventative infrastructure, something that supports physical and mental health, reduces inequalities, and strengthens community resilience. Targeted investment in areas like West Howe and Kinson deliberately prioritises those who have historically had least access to quality green space.

A model for towns and cities everywhere

As one of England's most densely populated urban areas, BCP's success in embedding nature into a constrained urban environment carries a powerful message for towns and cities facing similar pressures around growth, climate resilience, and public health. The question BCP has answered, not just in strategy documents but on the ground, is whether genuinely nature-rich urban places are achievable at scale. The answer is clearly yes.

Urban areas across the country are now taking the approaches pioneered here and adapting them to their own contexts, demonstrating that a greener, healthier, and more resilient urban future is within reach, wherever you are.

Eilish McGuinness, Chief Executive, The National Lottery Heritage Fund, said:

"It was fantastic to discover how closely council leaders, local charities, volunteers and community champions are working together to reimagine the role of nature in people’s everyday lives. BCP are creating a Nature Towns and Cities partnership model that will lead by example UK-wide, showing how investing in green spaces can strengthen local pride, improve natural heritage and biodiversity and drive economic growth. It’s thanks to players of the National Lottery that the Heritage Fund can spearhead funding to support urban communities in their drive to save our precious natural heritage for all to enjoy."

What BCP has pioneered, towns and cities across the country are now making their own. The model is scalable, the benefits are real, and the ambition is national. Over the next decade, Nature Towns and Cities will work with one hundred urban areas across the UK so that many more communities can enjoy the healthier, greener, more resilient places they deserve.

Visit the website to find out more: Home - Nature Towns and Cities

entry.title: Natural England publishes Hen Harrier Brood Management Trial
entry.summary: By Matthew Heard, National Delivery Director, Natural England Hen Harriers are one of the UK’s rarest birds of prey. However, they are at the centre of a long-running conflict because they prey on red grouse, which are managed for grouse …
entry.content:
By Matthew Heard, National Delivery Director, Natural England

Hen Harriers are one of the UK’s rarest birds of prey. However, they are at the centre of a long-running conflict because they prey on red grouse, which are managed for grouse shooting. To help address this problem, Natural England and its partners have explored approaches that could support both Hen Harrier conservation and sustainable grouse shooting. This blog explains the results of the 'brood management' trial, which concluded that this activity contributed to increased numbers of nesting Hen Harriers on some grouse moors, and presents the full evaluation report which has now been published.

Hen Harriers are iconic birds of upland landscapes, yet they remain at the centre of one of England’s most intractable human–wildlife conflicts. Despite being protected by law, they are illegally killed because they are predators of red grouse, and law enforcement alone has not been successful in improving their numbers. Therefore, we have been working with our partners to explore ways of reducing the impact of Hen Harriers on grouse shoots, to support thriving Hen Harrier populations that coexist with sustainable grouse shooting. One method, known as 'brood management', has been trialed in recent years as an avenue to improving tolerance of Hen Harriers on grouse moors.

What is Brood Management?  

Brood management reduces Hen Harrier nest density on grouse moors by temporarily removing the eggs and/or broods of chicks under licence, rearing them in captivity, and releasing the young birds back into the wild at a suitable location, once they are able to fly and disperse. Providing a lawful way to reduce predation of nesting Hen Harriers on grouse promotes coexistence between grouse moor interests and Hen Harriers. 

The Brood Management Trial – recap of the evidence gathered 

Brood management was trialed under licence in northern England between 2018 and 2024, through a partnership of Natural England, the Moorland Association, the International Centre for Birds of Prey, the Game & Wildlife Conservation Trust and the Hawk & Owl Trust.

The final reports of the trial have now been published.   

Headline results were published in 2025: 

  • During the trial, Hen Harrier numbers increased substantially in areas managed for grouse shooting where brood management was available (but not in other areas).
  • Illegal killing continued throughout the trial, but no crime hotspots were identified within brood management areas.
  • Although the act of safely rearing a small number of chicks in captivity probably made a small contribution to population growth, the numbers involved were too low to explain the increase in nesting pairs that took place over this period. Research by the British Trust for Ornithology suggests the increase was more likely driven by higher survival rates and greater settlement and breeding by wild birds. 
  • At the end of the trial, Natural England and its independent Natural England Science Advisory Committee (NESAC) concluded that the availability of brood management had probably contributed to population growth, primarily through reduced nest disturbance and improved settlement on some grouse moors.
  • NESAC advised that the widespread use and awareness of satellite tagging and monitoring as part of the trial likely contributed to reduced disturbance and improved breeding success. Importantly, the effects of the availability of brood management could not be fully separated from those of the accompanying tagging and monitoring programme.

Review of the evidence for brood management 

Natural England recognises that brood management is controversial. Concerns include whether brood management addresses the underlying drivers of illegal killing, whether it distracts from the need for effective law enforcement, and whether increases in Hen Harrier numbers are really due to brood management rather than increased monitoring and satellite tagging. 

Having carefully considered the available evidence and advice, Natural England's view is that the availability of brood management, including satellite tagging, monitoring and communication of bird locations likely contributed to improved breeding success in some areas. 

Current evidence supports use of brood management under licence where projects follow the methods used in the trial. This is likely to include satellite tagging and monitoring, subject to case-by-case assessment. Such projects should be for the explicit aim of increasing Hen Harrier numbers by reducing illegal killing and disturbance. 

Not a substitute for tackling wildlife crime  

More widely, brood management can be justified as a Hen Harrier conservation tool when used alongside diversionary feeding, engagement, enforcement, monitoring and research. It is not a substitute for directly tackling wildlife crime. 

These views are based on the currently available evidence, including the results of the Brood Management Trial, and will be kept under review as new evidence emerges. 

Acknowledgements and Further Reading 

Natural England would like to thank all the project partners who worked together on making the trial and evaluation possible, as well as the landowners who allowed access for release and monitoring. 

  • The final reports from the Hen Harrier Brood Management Trial have now been published here.  
  • Hen Harrier Brood Management Trial Evaluation: The effectiveness of brood management as a mechanism for supporting Hen Harrier recovery.  Natural England Research Report NERR153 
  • Hen Harrier Brood Management Trial: Interim social science evaluation. Natural England Research Report NERR160 
  • Hen Harrier Brood Management Trial: Findings from the social science survey of moorland managers Authors: National Centre for Social Research. Natural England Commission Report NECR615

entry.title: High Court judgment threatens protections for England’s internationally important wildlife sites
entry.summary: Natural England intends to appeal a High Court judgment arising from a judicial review brought by the British Association for Shooting and Conservation (BASC) concerning gamebird release licensing. Gamebird release licensing was introduced in 2021 to protect internationally important species …
entry.content:
Natural England intends to appeal a High Court judgment arising from a judicial review brought by the British Association for Shooting and Conservation (BASC) concerning gamebird release licensing.

Gamebird release licensing was introduced in 2021 to protect internationally important species and habitats found within Special Protection Areas (SPAs) and Special Areas of Conservation (SACs), collectively known as European Sites. A licence is required only where pheasants or red-legged partridges are released on, or within 500 metres of, one of these designated sites. Fewer than 1% of shoots in England are affected.

In recent years, Natural England has taken additional steps through the licensing regime to protect SPA bird populations from the risks posed by bird flu. The disease has caused unprecedented mortality in wild birds worldwide and poses a potentially catastrophic threat to the rare and internationally important species for which many SPAs are designated.

Since the emergence of bird flu, we have carefully considered the risks posed by the disease to protected species and habitats. Throughout this period, we have sought to minimise impacts on gamebird shoots and businesses while continuing to meet our obligations under the Habitats Regulations and wider conservation legislation.

The legal challenge

In September 2025, BASC brought a judicial review claim against Natural England.

The claim challenged licence conditions that restricted the keeping of gamebirds in release pens within SPAs and their 500m buffer zones before the beginning of the shooting season. Natural England imposed those conditions to reduce the risk of bird flu transmission from gamebirds, particularly pheasants, to protected wild bird populations. Natural England’s approach sought to minimise that risk by delaying releases until after breeding birds were expected largely to have left SPAs.

BASC argued that Natural England had used its licensing powers for a purpose not authorised by the relevant legislation and had incorrectly interpreted what constitutes a “release into the wild” under section 14 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981. BASC also challenged Natural England’s guidance that a licence would be required where a release pen falls partly within and partly outside a controlled zone.

Natural England’s position was that the conditions were imposed for the purpose Parliament intended: protecting vulnerable species and ensuring compliance with wildlife conservation law. We argued that there is a direct connection between keeping gamebirds in release pens and the licensed activity of releasing them into the wild, because the former activity is undertaken to facilitate the latter.

The case was heard on 1 and 2 July 2026.

The Court’s decision

The Court found that Natural England acted beyond its powers in imposing conditions that prevented the keeping of pheasants and partridges within pens in SPAs and their 500m buffer zones before the start of the shooting season. However, BASC’s challenge to Natural England’s guidance on release pens that straddle the boundaries of SPAs and their 500m buffer zones was rejected.

Why we are appealing

Natural England respectfully disagrees with the judgment and intends to appeal the decision on a number of points of law.

Protecting England’s internationally important wildlife sites and the species they support remains at the heart of our work, and we will continue to use every appropriate legal mechanism available to fulfil that responsibility.
